title: The Station Agent
full_review:
Three loners find friendship and emotional healing in an abandoned train depot in the well-written and well-acted "The Station Agent" (Miramax).

Writer-director Tom McCarthy rides the rails of the human heart in this tender meditation on loneliness and our underlying need for community.

Casting a shadow -- inversely proportionate to his diminutive size -- across the narrative is Finbar McBride (Peter Dinklage), a social misfit who works in a model train shop. Fin is a "railfan" -- a person obsessed with the history and lore of American railroads. But while the store affords him an ideal opportunity to indulge in his locomotive passions, it cannot shield him from the unwanted stares and cruel jokes brought on by his dwarfism.

Fin's life unexpectedly changes tracks when he inherits a ramshackle train station in the New Jersey countryside. Desperate for privacy, Fin decides to move into the hermit-friendly depot. But his cloistered solitude is soon shattered by encounters with two locals: Olivia (Patricia Clarkson), an emotionally fragile artist grieving the death of her young child, and Joe (Bobby Cannavale), a conversation-hungry vendor who, to Fin's dismay, parks his snack truck alongside the station.

Wanting nothing more than to be left alone, Fin is, at first, unresponsive to their overtures. Reluctantly, however, he is drawn into their emotional orbits. Slowly, his standoffish shell is cracked by the mutually healing balm of friendship, which Fin also extends to the town's lovelorn librarian (Michelle Williams) and Cleo (Raven Goodwin), a shy fifth-grader, who cajoles him into speaking to her class about trains.

Dinklage's calibrated performance quickly pulls viewers' attention away from his Lilliputian stature into the depth of his emotional range. And though a physically unconventional candidate for a leading man, he maintains a commanding presence throughout the film, even when playing against actors who tower over him, imbuing the role of Fin with a subtle blend of detached stoicism and disarming warmth.

On a societal level, the film serves to break the stereotyped perception which, in cinema, relegates dwarfs to playing curly-shoed court jesters, asexual Christmas ornaments or other assorted Fellini-esque set dressings, depriving them, in the minds of moviegoers, of humanity, and thus denying them the opportunity to express love, anger or grief.

"The Station Agent" also eloquently speaks to the wider human condition, and its underlying need for interpersonal bonds. Connecting people and communities separated by physical and emotional distances, railroads serve as an apt metaphor for the intersection of lives depicted in the film, with the station house itself being the hub where their isolated existences -- journeying along different life tracks -- meet in community.

This is one small film you might want to see before it pulls out of the station.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, an instance of drug abuse, and sporadic rough and crude language, as well as profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
